P1.title: Blink
P1.heading: The user LED and the BOOT button
P1.goal: Explore two on-board controls: blink the user LED on GPIO27 and read the BOOT button on GPIO28. Hold BOOT to change the blink rate.
steps: Nothing to wire: the LED and the BOOT button are on the board.
Run the command. The LED blinks twice a second.
Hold BOOT: the LED blinks fast and the monitor prints button pressed.
P1.note: GPIO27 and GPIO28 are strapping pins: the chip reads them at reset to pick its boot mode. Using them after boot is fine; holding BOOT during reset enters download mode.

micropython.label: MicroPython
micropython.goal: Blink the on-board LED on GPIO27 and read BOOT on GPIO28 with a MicroPython script. Hold BOOT to change the blink rate.
steps: Install MicroPython in lesson 00 if needed. Nothing to wire: the LED and BOOT button are on the board.
Open Code, connect the serial REPL and run gpio.py.
Hold BOOT: the LED blinks faster and the console reports the button state. Press Stop before changing the script.
micropython.note: GPIO27 and GPIO28 are strapping pins. Pressing BOOT after startup is fine; holding it during reset enters download mode.

P2.title: RGB mixer
P2.heading: Mix colours from the serial console
P2.goal: Send RGB values to the on-board WS2812, compare the primary colours and adjust brightness without uploading another sketch.
steps: Nothing to wire. Upload the sketch and open its serial monitor at 115200 baud.
Send rgb 255 0 0, rgb 0 255 0 and rgb 0 0 255 to compare the primary colours.
Send rgb 255 80 0, then level 20 and level 100. Compare colour and brightness; send off when done.
P2.note: No colour? Check that RGB_PIN is 0: the LED's data line is GPIO0, the D2/RGB pad.

micropython.label: MicroPython
micropython.goal: Mix colours on the on-board WS2812 from the MicroPython REPL without changing or uploading the script for every colour.
steps: Nothing to wire. Open Code, connect the serial REPL and run rgb_mixer.py.
In the terminal, send rgb 255 0 0, rgb 0 255 0 and rgb 0 0 255 to compare the primary colours.
Send rgb 255 80 0, then level 20 and level 100. Send off and press Stop when finished.
micropython.note: The RGB data line is GPIO0 (D2/RGB). If the LED stays dark, check that RGB_PIN is 0.

P3.title: Analog in
P3.heading: Read a voltage with the ADC
P3.goal: Turn a potentiometer on A2 and watch the 12-bit ADC follow it, in raw counts and in calibrated millivolts.
steps: Unplug USB, then wire the potentiometer as shown in the diagram.
Plug in and run the command.
Turn the knob end to end: raw goes from about 0 to 4095, millivolts from about 0 to 3100.
Open Tools → Serial Plotter to see both lines move.
P3.note: The board drawing boxes all six ADC channels. For your own sensors use A2 (GPIO4) and A3 (GPIO5); A1 and A6 work too when nothing is plugged into QWIIC. Never feed more than 3.3 V into them.

micropython.label: MicroPython
micropython.goal: Turn a potentiometer on A2 and read its scaled 16-bit value and approximate voltage with MicroPython.
steps: Disconnect USB, then wire the potentiometer exactly as shown in the diagram.
Reconnect USB, open Code, connect the serial REPL and run adc.py.
Turn the knob end to end. Compare the 0–65535 scaled reading with the millivolt value in the terminal; press Stop when done.
micropython.note: The millivolt reading is approximate and can saturate near 3.3 V. Never apply more than 3.3 V to A2.

P4.title: On-board sensors
P4.heading: Scan the sensor I²C bus
P4.goal: Start the I²C bus that links the chip to the board's five sensors and list who answers: pressure, temperature and humidity, proximity and light, magnetic field and battery.
steps: Nothing to wire: the sensors and their 4.7 kΩ pull-ups are on the board.
Run the command. Every five seconds the monitor lists the devices found.
Compare the list with the table.
P4.note: This bus is separate from the QWIIC connector (GPIO1 and GPIO6), which the Sensors lessons use for external boards.

micropython.label: MicroPython
micropython.short: Bus scanner and one script per sensor
micropython.goal: Use MicroPython to scan the Pulsar C5's on-board sensor bus, then read each of the five sensors with its own driver.
steps: Nothing to wire: the five sensors and pull-up resistors are on the board.
Open Code, connect the serial REPL and run i2c_scan.py. Compare the addresses with the table.
Pick a sensor tab: mmc5603_compass.py, max17048_battery.py, fht40_temp_humidity.py, lps22hb_pressure.py or vcnl4040_light_prox.py.
Press Install for its driver once, then Run on board. Breathe on the board, cover the light sensor or turn it near a magnet and watch the values change. Press Stop when finished.
micropython.note: This on-board bus uses GPIO2/GPIO3. The QWIIC connector uses a separate bus on GPIO1/GPIO6. The battery script needs a LiPo cell connected.

P5.title: microSD
P5.heading: Write a file over SPI
P5.goal: Mount the microSD card over SPI, append a line on every boot and read the whole file back.
steps: Format a microSD card as FAT32 and push it into the slot.
Run the command. The monitor prints the card size and the file.
Press RST a few times: one more boot at … ms line each time.
P5.note: SCK shares GPIO27 with the user LED, so the LED flickers while the card is busy. That is expected.

micropython.label: MicroPython
micropython.goal: Mount the on-board microSD card with MicroPython, append a line to a file and read it back.
steps: Format a microSD card as FAT32 and insert it fully into the on-board slot.
Open Code, connect serial and select Install sdcard.py. This saves UNIT's SPI driver on the board.
Run microsd.py. The script uses SPI on GPIO27/7/26/23 and mounts the card at /sd.
Run the script again: /sd/pulsar.txt should contain one more line while retaining the first.
micropython.note: This MicroPython example imports UNIT's sdcard.py from the board filesystem. Install it once from the code workspace before running. GPIO27 is shared with the user LED, which may flicker during card access.

P6.title: UART
P6.heading: Loop a serial port back to itself
P6.goal: Send what you type out of TX0 and read it back on RX0 through one jumper, while the USB port stays your console.
steps: Unplug USB and put one jumper between TX0 and RX0.
Plug in and run the command.
Type a line and press Enter: it comes back as loopback: ….
Pull the jumper: nothing comes back.
P6.note: To talk to another board instead, cross the wires (TX → RX, RX → TX) and join the grounds.

micropython.label: MicroPython
micropython.goal: Send a line from the USB REPL through UART1 on GPIO11 and read it back on GPIO12 with one jumper.
steps: Disconnect USB and bridge TX0 (GPIO11) to RX0 (GPIO12) with one jumper, then reconnect USB.
Open Code, connect the serial REPL and run uart_loopback.py.
Type hello UART in the terminal and send it. The script prints loopback: hello UART.
Remove the jumper and send another line: the script reports no response. Press Stop when done.
micropython.note: The USB REPL stays separate from UART1. For another board, cross TX and RX and connect grounds.
